extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and physicists (readers of Newton's Principia); scholars of classical mechanics
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction and summarization of propositions/theorems from a Latin treatise on motion under centripetal forces (Newtonian Principia style). Focused on conditions for isochronous oscillation, area-time relations, two-body and many-body attraction results, and methods for constructing trajectories and times by geometric quadratures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocities and times of pendulums in cycloids (Prop. LII / Problem XXXIV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definire & velocitates pendulorum in locis singulis, & tempora quibus tum oscillationes totce, tum singula oscillationum partes peraguntur. (Find velocities of pendulums at single locations, and the times in which whole oscillations and parts of oscillations are performed.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct semicircle and compare cycloidal arcs with circular arcs; relate velocity at a point T to velocity at lowest point R by ratios of ordinates applied to the radius (ordinatim applicata LI ad radium GK) and arc proportions (JSRq.—TRq. ad SR). For unequal oscillations, arcs described in equal times are proportional to the whole arcs of the oscillations; from given times one obtains velocities and arcs in general oscillations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isochronism of pendulums in related cycloids (Corollary to Prop. LII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oscillationes in globis & cycloidibus omnibus, quibuscunque cum viribus absolutis factae, sunt in ratione quae componitur ex subduplicata ratione longitudinis directe, & subduplicata ratione distantiae inter punctum suspensionis & centrum globi inverse, & subduplicata ratione vis absolutae globi etiam inverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Period of oscillation composes as: direct subduplicate (i.e. sqrt) of length, inverse subduplicate of distance from suspension point to globe center, and inverse subduplicate of the absolute force of the globe. Special limiting cases recover known results for the common cycloid and circular pendulum (Wrennius & Huygens). Useful to compare times of descent to times of semi-oscillation by geometric limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forces making oscillations isochronous on a given curve (Prop. LIII / Problem XXXV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concessis figurarum curvilinearum quadraturis, invenire vires quibus corpora in datis curvis lineis oscillationes semper isochronas peragent. (Given quadratures of curves, find forces that make oscillations on those curves always isochronous.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At a point T on curve, draw tangent TX and take TY equal to the arc TR; erect perpendicular YZ, draw CT through Z; then the centripetal force that produces isochronous oscillations is proportional to the perpendicular TZ. Decompose that force into tangential and normal components: the tangential parallel to the filament does not change motion along the curve, while the normal component TY effects the required acceleration/retardation along the curve. The construction depends on known quadratures (arc lengths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Isochronous force for a simple pendulum (Corollary to Prop. LIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body T on a straight rod AT describes an arc of a circle TRQ and is urged downward by a force composed with gravity so that the total downward force is proportional to the line arising from the rectangle under arc TR and radius AR and the sine TN, then the single oscillation times are equal (isochronous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In horology: if machine-impressed forces can be combined with gravity so total downward force at each position is proportional to the applied rectangle under arc and radius (or to the arc's sine), all oscillations are isochronous. Use the geometric relation between tangent constructions and the sine of the arc to design escapements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Times of descent/ascent along arbitrary curves using quadratures (Prop. LIV / Problem XXXVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concessis figurarum curvilinearum quadraturis, invenire tempora, quibus corpora vi qualibet centripeta in lineis quibuscunque curvis, in plano per centrum virium transeunte descriptis, descendent & ascendent. (Given quadratures of curves and a centripetal law, find the times bodies descend and ascend along given curved paths in a plane through the center.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide the radius CS into innumerable equal parts; for each part construct a circle and the short line element of the curve cutting that circle. Using the given centripetal law and altitude from which the body fell, determine the velocity at any altitude (per prop. XXXIX). Time to traverse a small element is proportional to its length and inversely proportional to velocity; assign to each element a perpendicular DN and area DN·nd proportional to time. Thus the total area under a constructed curve (P N n etc.) gives the time for descent along S T. The method reduces time computation to area/quadrature problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal-area (area-time) law for motion on a curved surface (Prop. LV / Theorem XIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body moves on any curved surface whose axis passes through the center of forces, and from the body a perpendicular to the axis is drawn and a parallel to it equal and drawn from a fixed axis point, then that parallel describes an area proportional to time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project the motion's trace into a plane perpendicular to axis; resolve the centripetal force into components and consider only the component acting in that plane. The motion in that plane is equivalent to motion under a single centripetal force toward the axis' center; hence by proposition I the sector/area described by the radius in that plane is proportional to time. The result generalizes the area-time law (Kepler's law) to motions constrained to surfaces whose axis goes through the force center.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing trajectories on a curved surface from quadratures and centripetal law (Prop. LVI / Problem XXXVII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given quadratures and both the centripetal law to a given center and the curved surface whose axis passes through that center, determine the trajectory a body will describe on that surface from a given point with given velocity in a given direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the area-time proportionality: for a given small time the area POp described in the projection plane is known; this gives the angle POp and hence the intersection point of an ellipse (constructed with given circle Tt data) and the line OP; repeating yields the trace APp in the plane and lifting perpendicularly to the surface gives trajectory points T. The method reduces trajectory construction to repeated ellipse/line intersections and area computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual attractions treated as centripetal to common center (Section XI principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attractions between bodies are mutual and equal (third law), so bodies attracted mutually revolve about a common center of gravity; in mathematical treatment centripetal forces may be considered as attractions to that common center even if physically impulses are more accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To treat many-body problems mathematically, consider centripetal forces as attractions to a common (possibly moving) center of gravity; neglecting the physical subtleties, one can use the same geometric constructions as for attraction to a fixed center, suitably translating by the center's uniform motion if it moves uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two bodies attract and describe similar figures about common center (Prop. LVII / Theorem XX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two bodies mutually attracting describe, about their common center of gravity and about one another, figures that are similar. (Distances of the bodies from the common center are reciprocally proportional to the bodies.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because distances from the common center are reciprocally proportional to masses, lines joining bodies to the center maintain given ratios and equal angular motion; hence the loci described around their respective terminals are similar. Use equal angular motion and proportional linear scales to infer similarity of the paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of mutual trajectories under arbitrary laws (Prop. LVIII / Theorem XXI)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two bodies, attracted mutually by arbitrary forces, revolve about their common center, then the curves one body describes about the other can be similar and equal to the curves described about the common center under appropriate proportional relations of forces and distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct equal and parallel displacements and compare tangents and arcs; by similarity of figures and proportionality of forces (or equality when bodies are equal) one shows that motion produced by the posterior force yields a curve similar to that produced by the prior force. Consider cases where the center is at rest or moving uniformly to extend the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of periodic times to masses (Prop. LIX / Theorem XXII)
rubrics_metrics.description: For two bodies S and P revolving about their common center, the periodic time of one relative to the periodic time of the other (around the other as if it were fixed) is in the subduplicate (square-root) ratio of the other body to the sum S+P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From previous theorems, times of describing similar arcs are in subduplicate ratio of the distances to the center, which reduce to ratios involving the masses and their sum; composing these ratios gives the relationship between full periods. Use this to compare orbital periods and to infer scaling with combined mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse-square centripetal law implies conic sections and axis scaling (Prop. LX / Theorem XXIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two bodies attract mutually with centripetal forces proportional to the reciprocal of the square of the distance, then the ellipses described about the common center and about each other have principal axes related by ratios involving the masses and their sum (axes scale according to means between masses and their sum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ellipses are equal, periods are in subduplicate ratio; changing the period in one ellipse changes the principal axis in a sesquiplicate ratio leading to axis relations expressed via means (medii proportionals) between the sum S+P and the individual masses. This yields how axes change when considering motion about the moving vs. fixed center.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence to attraction by a single center (Prop. LXI / Theorem XXIV)
rubrics_metrics.description: If bodies mutually attract by any laws, however they move otherwise, their motions will behave as if they were not attracting each other but each were attracted by a third body placed at the common center of gravity by forces of the same law with respect to distance from that center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mutual attractions tend toward the common center; therefore their resultant is the same as if all attractions emanated from an intermediate center. Hence one may replace mutual attraction with equivalent attraction to the common center with the same distance-law for mathematical determination of motions (useful for reduction of many-body problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of many-body inverse-square system to central problem (Prop. LXII / Problem XXXVIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: For bodies whose mutual forces are reciprocal-square with distance and which are released from given places, determine motions: treat bodies as if drawn to a single body placed at the common gravitational center, which by hypothesis remains at rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the theorem that bodies move as though attracted by the common center; set that center at rest by hypothesis and reduce to previously solved central-force problems (problems 9 & 26 referenced). Thus motions of mutually attracting bodies with inverse-square law are obtained from the central-force solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of two-body motions using center-of-mass reduction (Prop. LXIII / Problem XXXIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two bodies attracting by inverse-square law, from given places, along given lines, with given exit velocities, determine their motions by reducing to motion of each about the common center moving uniformly and then composing with uniform translation of the system's space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From initial data obtain uniform motion of the common center and the bodies' initial motions relative to that center; subsequent motions are as if each were attracted to that center (per earlier problems). Combine the resulting central motions with the uniform motion of the center to obtain absolute motions in fixed space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing motions for multiple attracting bodies by composition (Prop. LXIV / Problem XL)
rubrics_metrics.description: When attractions between bodies increase in simple ratio of distances to centers, determine motions of many bodies among themselves: bodies may describe ellipses about successive centers and compose motions by adding further attracting bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with two-body ellipses about common center D; when a third body is added and mutual accelerative attractions resolved, the resultant central accelerative components about D produce new ellipses with changed speeds. Repeating the construction and adding further bodies yields motions for many bodies. The method composes centripetal contributions and uses corollaries about area/time and parallelling accelerative components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate validity of elliptical motions for spherical bodies with inverse-square forces (Prop. LXV / Theorem XXV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spherical bodies whose forces decrease in duplicate ratio of distance may move among themselves in ellipses, and radii to umbilici describe areas approximately proportional to times, under conditions where perturbations are small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If small bodies revolve about a very large mass (maximum), or if mutual perturbing accelerations are negligible, the small bodies move in ellipses and areas are nearly proportional to times. Provide two cases: (1) sufficiently small orbiting bodies so maximum remains essentially fixed; (2) system of small bodies where the maximum is far and the system's internal inclinations and unequal accelerations are made negligible. The result quantifies approximation errors and suggests how to make them arbitrarily small by reducing perturbing masses or increasing distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perturbation effects and conditions for area-time proportionality (Prop. LXVI / Theorem XXVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: If bodies' forces decrease as duplicate ratio of distances and additional accelerative attractions among some bodies are reciprocally proportional to squares of distances, then inner small bodies revolve more nearly in elliptical form and their area-time proportionality improves when the large attracting mass acts on them by those attractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed cases show how adding large distant attractors or changing magnitudes of accelerative attractions affects the closeness to ideal elliptical motion. The theorem lays out how inclinations, unequal actions, and non-quadratic proportionalities increase perturbations, and conversely how arranging reciprocal-square accelerations and limiting relative sizes/distances reduces errors and brings trajectories closer to exact ellipses and exact area-time proportionality.
